content: Estrogen use increases the risk of developing endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining. The longer you use estrogen, the higher the risk. If you have not had a hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus), your doctor may prescribe a progestin to take alongside vaginal estrogen. This combination may reduce the risk of endometrial cancer but could increase the risk of other health issues, such as breast cancer. Before starting vaginal estrogen, inform your doctor if you have or have ever had cancer or if you experience unusual vaginal bleeding. If you notice abnormal or unusual vaginal bleeding during treatment, contact your doctor immediately. Large studies have shown that women who take oral estrogen combined with progestins have a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, blood clots in the lungs or legs, breast cancer, and dementia. Women using vaginal estrogen, either alone or with progestins, may also face an increased risk of these conditions. Inform your doctor if you smoke, have had a heart attack or stroke in the past year, or if you or a family member has a history of blood clots or breast cancer. Be vigilant for symptoms that could indicate serious health conditions. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following while using vaginal estrogen: sudden, severe headache or vomiting; speech difficulties; dizziness or fainting; sudden loss of vision or double vision; weakness or numbness in an arm or leg; crushing chest pain or heaviness; coughing up blood; sudden shortness of breath; difficulty thinking, remembering, or learning; breast lumps or changes; nipple discharge; or pain, tenderness, or redness in one leg. To minimize risks, do not use vaginal estrogen, with or without progestin, to prevent heart disease, heart attacks, strokes, or dementia. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to manage your symptoms. Consult your doctor every 3-6 months to determine whether you should lower your dose or discontinue the medication. Perform monthly breast self-exams and schedule annual mammograms and breast exams with your doctor to detect breast cancer early. Your doctor may recommend more frequent exams based on your personal or family medical history. If you are scheduled for surgery or will be on bed rest, inform your doctor. They may advise you to stop using vaginal estrogen 4-6 weeks beforehand to reduce the risk of blood clots. Regularly discuss the risks and benefits of vaginal estrogen use with your doctor. Vaginal estrogen is prescribed to treat symptoms such as vaginal dryness, itching, burning, painful or difficult urination, and sudden urgency to urinate in postmenopausal women. The Femring® vaginal ring is also used to treat hot flashes in menopausal women. Premarin® vaginal cream is used to treat kraurosis vulvae, a condition causing vaginal dryness and discomfort in women or girls of any age. Vaginal estrogen belongs to a class of medications called hormones and works by replacing the estrogen naturally produced by the body. Vaginal estrogen is available as a flexible ring, a tablet, or a cream. Vaginal rings are typically left in place for three months before being replaced if treatment is still needed. Vaginal tablets are usually inserted daily for the first two weeks, then twice weekly as needed. Vaginal creams are applied daily for 2-4 weeks, then 1-3 times weekly. Always use vaginal estrogen at the same time each day and follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Do not use more or less than prescribed. To insert a vaginal ring, wash and dry your hands, remove the ring from its pouch, and choose a comfortable position (e.g., standing with one leg raised, squatting, or lying down). Squeeze the ring into a figure-eight shape, hold open the vaginal folds, and insert the ring as far back as possible. If the ring falls out, wash it with warm water and reinsert it. If it is lost, insert a new ring. The ring can remain in place during sexual activity, but if removed, it should be washed and reinserted promptly. To remove the ring, hook a finger through it and gently pull it out. Dispose of the ring in the trash, not the toilet. To use vaginal tablets, remove an applicator from its packaging, load the tablet, and insert the applicator into the vagina as far as comfortable. Press the plunger to release the tablet, then dispose of the applicator. For vaginal cream, attach the applicator to the cream tube, fill it to the prescribed dose, and insert it into the vagina. Press the plunger to release the cream, then clean the applicator with mild soap and warm water. Before using vaginal estrogen, inform your doctor if you are allergic to estrogen products or any of their ingredients. Provide a list of all medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as some may interact with vaginal estrogen. Notify your doctor if you have a history of conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, asthma, migraines, seizures, porphyria, or thyroid, liver, kidney, gallbladder, or pancreatic disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor immediately. Note that some estrogen creams may weaken latex or rubber birth control devices, such as condoms or diaphragms. Store vaginal estrogen at room temperature, away from heat and moisture, and out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services. Symptoms of overdose may include upset stomach, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding. Common side effects of vaginal estrogen include breast tenderness, nausea, heartburn, dizziness, mood changes, hair loss, leg cramps, and vaginal irritation. Serious side effects, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, severe abdominal pain, or difficulty breathing, require immediate medical attention. Estrogen use may increase the risk of ovarian cancer or gallbladder disease and may affect growth and sexual development in children. Discuss all risks with your doctor and report any unusual symptoms. Brand names for vaginal estrogen include Estrace®, Estring®, Femring®, Premarin®, and Vagifem®. Other names include conjugated estrogens and estradiol. Always consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information or clarification.
